title: API versioning and compatibility
idea: Backward compatibility means old clients keep working after you change an API; versioning gives a breaking change a new name, so both shapes can live side by side.
points: Adding an optional field is safe; removing or renaming one breaks clients.
Keep one internal model and map it to each public version.
Old clients should ignore unknown fields: the tolerant reader rule.
Deprecate a version with notice before removing it, never silently.

hero.caption: Additive changes are usually safe. Anything that takes away or reshapes data needs a new version.

code.title: One model, two versions
code.caption: Add a `v3` presenter that also returns `currency` at the top level. `v1` and `v2` stay untouched.

walk.text: The domain object has one shape, the newest one.
`v1` rebuilds the old shape: a flat name and a decimal total.
`v2` exposes the richer shape. Old clients never see it.
An unknown version gets a clear 400, not a guess.

code.title: A tolerant reader
code.caption: Destructuring picks known fields and ignores new ones. A default hides a removed field, but the answer is wrong.

pitfalls: Never rename a field in place; add the new one and deprecate the old.
Do not fork the domain model per version; map one model at the edge.
Clients that reject unknown fields turn every additive change into a breaking one.

quiz.why: `v1` divides cents by 100. `v2` has no `total` field, so the destructuring default `'none'` is used.

takeaway: Add freely, never take away in place; version the breaking change.
